subtopic: LEBANON

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: LEBANON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a statement to make on UNOGIL and the Lebanese election.
Hon. members have no doubt already heard that the Lebanese chamber of deputies has elected General Fouad Chehab as the next president of the Republic of Lebanon. We in Canada sincerely welcome his election, both because of the widespread respect which he enjoys both inside and outside Lebanon and also because of the reassuring evidence afforded by his election that the Lebanese people are determined to put an end to the difficulties which have unhappily divided them in recent months. We express the hope that the transitional period before the new president takes office will pass peaceably and without further disturbances. We trust that under his presidency the task of the United Nations observation group will continue to be facilitated, and that UNOGIL will be able to contribute to conditions of stability that will render easier the task undertaken by the general.
On July 22 mention was made in this chamber of the increasing effectiveness of the United Nations observation group in Lebanon. It was announced then that in response to a request by the Secretary General of the United Nations the government was assigning an additional three Canadian officers for service with UNOGIL and that
attention would be given to any further requirements as events transpired. There is every indication that despite the Soviet veto on July 22 of the resolution proposed by Japan-that was the resolution within the security council-it has been possible .for UNOGIL, within the authority granted it by the security council resolution of June 11, to expand the scope and area of its operations.
We have now received a further request from the secretary general for additional assistance, and in response have agreed to assign an additional seven Canadian officers. This will bring to 20 the number of officers -in a total force of some 200-sent from Canada to help in this operation.
It is encouraging to note that so far 20 countries have been approached to provide personnel for UNOGIL, indicating the breadth of the international base that is being sought and achieved for this exercise which we believe will bring about the preservation of peace.

subtopic: SUMMIT CONFERENCE-PROPOSED MEETING ON AUGUST 12

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: SUMMIT CONFERENCE-PROPOSED MEETING ON AUGUST 12
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish also to take this opportunity to say something in regard to the heads of government meeting and the security council. The Prime Minister of the United Kingdom announced in the House of Commons at Westminster today that in the reply he has sent to Mr. Khrushchev's message of July 28 he has suggested that the proposed high level meeting of the security council be held on August 12, the place and details of the meeting to be worked out in the security council by the permanent representatives of the member states. The Canadian government welcomes the positive stand taken by Mr. Macmillan, a stand which is fully in conformity with the position I have taken ever since the suggestion for a summit conference on the Middle East was put forward.
As has been made clear in the House of Commons on more than one occasion, the government of Canada stands ready today to do all in its power to promote the successful completion of the steps now contemplated to the end that this meeting may take place. If the security council, of which Canada is currently a member, is in fact convened at heads of government level on August 12 in New York or elsewhere, I shall be ready to

External Affairs
attend. If Canada can make any contribution to the success of the proposed conference, and that includes the convening of the meeting of the security council at the summit, that contribution will be made willingly and with full confidence that it will have the approval of all those who are sincerely dedicated to the cause of peace.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: SUMMIT CONFERENCE-PROPOSED MEETING ON AUGUST 12
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members of the house and certainly hon. members on this side will welcome the news the Prime Minister was good enough to give the house to the effect that the representatives Of the people of Lebanon have chosen a president in the person of a distinguished Lebanese patriot. We must hope that this step will help bring to an end the civil disturbances in Lebanon and restore peace and stability in that country, and thereby make possible the withdrawal of outside forces, in this case forces from the United States of America.
I noted with interest what the Prime Minister said about the strengthening of the United Nations observation group. That strengthening should make it possible for the group to discharge its functions in Lebanon, which in turn would make it still easier for the United States forces to withdraw. We most warmly support the decision of the government to add another seven officers to that peace preservation corps under the flag of the United Nations. I can think of no way in which the Canadian army through its officers could better act in the present circumstances than as part of this peace preservation corps.
So far as the summit conference is concerned, we welcome also the information that it is now likely to be convened very shortly, and I reiterate the hope already expressed that after an initial meeting of the full security council, which without doubt will be subject to a great deal of publicity, perhaps those governments most concerned will be able to meet in some manner under the auspices of the United Nations in as much privacy as they can obtain, and not only make a contribution to the solution of the immediate crisis in the Middle East but begin a process of settlement by international agreement, including all the governments concerned, covering those political and economic problems which have plagued that area for so many years and which, if not settled, will undoubtedly before long result in another crisis in that part of the world.

subtopic: SUMMIT CONFERENCE-PROPOSED MEETING ON AUGUST 12
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this group are pleased with the further indication that there is a relaxation of the

tension in Lebanon because it has been possible to elect a new president. We, of course, welcome wholeheartedly the announcement that UNOGIL will be strengthened in that area. We know that Canadians will support unanimously an increase in Canada's contribution. We express the hope that Canada will encourage the United States to withdraw its troops from this state as early as possible. We feel that the presence of United States troops in Lebanon has added to tension and is continuing to add to tension, and that they should be substituted by a strengthened UNOGIL immediately.
We welcome also the announcement by the United Kingdom that she is prepared to take part in a summit meeting, beginning August 12, at the United Nations. We express the hope that this summit meeting will be fruitful, that it will deal with the basic problems facing the people of this area, and that from that meeting will come not only arrangements for the withdrawal of the troops of the United States and the United Kingdom but also a program formulated for economic development that will result in the oil resources in that area being developed in the interests of the people who reside in those nations. We further express the hope that from the summit meeting will come an agreement which will lead to free elections in those nations so the people themselves may control their political as well as their economic destinies.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON REQUEST FOR FURTHER ECONOMIC AID

speakeroldname: Hon. Sidney E. Smith (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT ON REQUEST FOR FURTHER ECONOMIC AID
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, late in May the Canadian government received an urgent appeal from the government of Ceylon for economic aid, which it will require in order to finance a broad development program designed to strengthen its economy and provide a substantial increase in the standard of living of its people. Subsequently discussions have taken place between the ministers and officials of the governments of Canada and Ceylon concerning the nature of the assistance which Canada might contribute.
On the basis of these discussions, and having in mind the request made by Ceylon, it was decided to offer Ceylon a loan of $2 million to finance the purchase of 25,000 tons of flour and to make an outright grant of 5,000 tons of flour valued at $400,000.
I take this opportunity to inform the house that the government of Ceylon has decided to take up this loan and grant, and the shipment of the first 10,000 tons of flour will be made before the end of December of this year. The remainder of the flour

being made available under the loan and the grant will be shipped in the first quarter of 1959.
It will be recalled that on January 8 of this year my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce announced that a $15 million grant of flour and wheat would be made to India, Pakistan and Ceylon, and that $35 million in credit for the purchase of wheat and flour would be available upon request to all Colombo plan countries. Of the $15 million grant Ceylon received $3 million worth of flour.
In February last a loan of $25 million was made to India leaving $10 million uncommitted, and it is from this sum that the current loan to Ceylon is to be financed. The terms of the loan are identical with those covering the loan to India, that is the loan is repayable in seven equal annual instalments, with the first payment due at the end of the second year. It will bear interest at the rate of 4J per cent, payable annually.
I add to this statement that in the course of these discussions it was a matter of concern that the flour that Canada was being asked to provide to Ceylon might seriously jeopardize Australia's normal sale of wheat and flour to Ceylon. We have received firm assurances from the governments of Australia and Ceylon that the flour which we are now making available under the current loan and grant will not affect adversely Australia's interests.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the minister whether this particular grant to Ceylon, which we on this side support, is additional to the grant to India and Pakistan previously announced, and additional to the Colombo plan contribution?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is correct, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-STATEMENT ON PRESSURE TO CURTAIL IMPORTS OF ALUMINUM

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Sidney E. Smith (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: UNITED STATES-STATEMENT ON PRESSURE TO CURTAIL IMPORTS OF ALUMINUM
speechtext:
Yesterday the Leader of the Opposition asked me a question with respect to the export of aluminum from Canada to the United States. My answer is that the government is aware of the efforts of primary aluminum producers in the United States to seek relief from the effects of a general decline in the level of their production. It is my understanding that one of the points raised by the United States industry is the adverse effect of Soviet sales of aluminum in world markets at cut-rate prices. These sales have also affected our exports.
While there has not been any direct attempt on the part of United States producers to identify their difficulties with imports of aluminum from Canada, the submission made by the producers to the United States administration proposed that there should be a regulation of imports from foreign countries. Any restrictions imposed on the import of aluminum into the United States or any action to raise the duty on aluminum would, of course, cause substantial damage to our Canadian interests.
It was with that thought in mind that we raised this matter in the discussions we had when the President and the Secretary of State of the United States were in Ottawa earlier this month. Our representatives in Washington are following developments closely, and the house can be assured that we shall take whatever action may be necessary to bring our views to the attention of the United States government.

speechtext:
I
wish to address a question to the Acting Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources based on a newspaper report that caused my body temperature to rise as a conservation enthusiast. In view of newspaper reports to the effect that in the Yukon fires are being allowed to sweep through the country unchallenged, except where they threaten homes, would the minister inform the house whether this statement is correct? If so, would the minister inform the house whether consideration has been given to the use of armed forces personnel for firefighting purposes in order to limit as far as possible the destruction of our forest resources in the Yukon?

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Acting Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
subtopic: STEPS TAKEN TO FIGHT FOREST FIRES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources I should like to reply to this question. Before doing so, however, I should like to say that the hon. member for Yukon has been in daily touch with the minister and the department in connection with these fires.
I can assure the hon. member for Kootenay West that not only has consideration been given to the possibility he suggests but that members of the armed forces and of the R.C.M.P. have been actively engaged in the firefighting effort, and have made a tremendous contribution in helping to limit as far as possible the destruction of our forest resources in the Yukon.
It should also be made perfectly clear that firefighting activities have not been limited to those fires which threaten federal housing. In such a vast area so sparsely populated it is, of course, not possible to fight every single fire. Consequently it has been necessary to concentrate efforts on those fires which threaten the most valuable forest resources and, of course, those which endanger human life and property.
Under the direction of the commissioner of the Yukon Territory great efforts are being made to bring the fires under control. In addition to the regular force of forestry officers and members of the armed forces and of the R.C.M.P., a good deal of equipment and extra

personnel have been brought in from outside, notably from several of the national parks. Above all, tribute should be paid to the civilian population of the territory, who are bending every effort to help bring these fires under control.
The house will be pleased to learn that, in part because of the coming of rain but in very large measure because of the exceptional efforts of everyone participating in the firefighting activities, the threat has been greatly diminished in recent weeks, and the worst of the fires have been largely contained.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister of Fisheries, not only on my own account but also on behalf of the member for New Westminster, if there is going to be an advance in the time of fishing between the Pattullo bridge in New Westminster and the Mission bridge on the Fraser river?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacLean (Minister of Fisheries):
subtopic: FRASER RIVER, B.C.-REQUEST FOR EXTENSION OF SEASON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, both the hon. member for Fraser Valley and the hon. member for New Westminster have given me notice of intention to ask almost identical questions on this matter.
This is a matter which has been brought to my attention from time to time during the last year by those especially interested, and as a result I have had a thorough investigation made of this salmon fishery between the New Westminster bridge and the Mission bridge over the Fraser river which, under subsection 14 of section 67 of the British Columbia fishery regulations, must ordinarily close on September 15 of each year. My object
Inquiries of the Ministry was to determine whether the season in the area might be extended without endangering conservation.
The problem is complicated, as there are five species of salmon involved in this fishery. Each is constituted of a race which runs at a different time and to a different river. It is obvious from the reports that early closure has benefited some runs to a slight extent, while others do not appear to be affected. I feel that the analysis must be carried further before a final decision is reached and this will be done.
For the year 1958, however, action has been taken to amend the regulations to permit salmon fishing in the area concerned, but of course subject to the provision that the area director of the fisheries department in British Columbia may use the over-all powers given to 'him under the regulations to prohibit fishing for part or all the season, should it be determined that such action is necessary for the protection and proper escapement of the salmon to the spawning grounds.

Mr. Chairman, this resolution has to do with amendments to the Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act. Hon. members will recall that this act was given royal assent in May, 1953. Its basic purpose is to ensure that children are not deprived of higher education because of their father's death, where the death is determined by the Canadian pension commission to be related to service.
Briefly, the act provides for the payment, up to the age of 25 years, on behalf of a child who is following a course of higher education, of tuition fees and an allowance of $25 a month is granted for a period of four academic years or 36 months, whichever is the lesser.
The number of children who have already received benefits under this act has been somewhat higher than had been estimated, and that is all to the good. During the course of administration of the act certain anomalies and deficiencies have come to light, and it is hoped that these will be remedied by the proposed amendments which are contained in the bill to be introduced if this resolution is adopted. I shall now indicate very briefly the purport of these amendments.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ALLOWANCE AND EXTEND BENEFITS
speechtext: I wonder if I could ask hon. members to lower their voices. It is impossible to hear the minister.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ALLOWANCE AND EXTEND BENEFITS
speechtext:
Eligibility under the present act is restricted to a child on whose behalf a pension is being, or has been, paid because the parent's death is connected with war service. This has been found to be too restrictive. For example, it excludes a child who is over the age of 21 years at the time of the parent's death and who is already pursuing a course

Children of War Dead Act of higher education. It also excludes a child whose parent's death is compensable under a workmen's compensation act, or by legal liability on some person to pay damages, and the amount collected is such as to preclude the payment of pension which would otherwise be paid.
It further excludes a child whose parent's death is service-connected but, because of some technicality preventing payment of pension under the usual section of the Pension Act, an award is made by the commission under the compassionate clause. It excludes a child whose parent's death is found by the Canadian pension commission to be a direct result of a specific military duty in peacetime. And, finally, it excludes the child of a veteran who upon discharge from the forces is passed directly to my department for treatment and dies during such treatment. The Pension Act provides that in these circumstances pension is awarded to eligible dependents.
The bill which will be introduced later would extend eligibility for education assistance to the groups that I have mentioned. None of the groups is very large, but to the individual child his eligibility is of great importance. The government feels that justice and equity will be served by the proposed amendments, and I wish to point out that they preserve the principle of relationship of death to service.
Another amendment, and this I consider a very necessary and important one, would permit payment of the allowance at a rate of $60 a month where pension has ceased at the twenty-first birthday of the child. Prior to that age, pension would normally have been paid at $40 a month and an allowance of $25 is granted under the Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act. Experience has shown that the sharp decline in income upon discontinuance of pension is inadvisable, and it is proposed to adjust the situation by paying an allowance at the same rate that was granted to the single veteran student taking higher education under the Veterans Rehabilitation Act.

As I understand the statement made by the minister, the resolution divides itself under two heads; that is, first, it is sought here to extend the benefits of the act known as the Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act to classes of persons other than those now covered by the act and, second, also to increase the allowances that may be paid in certain cases as the minister has set out.

I have also listened with interest to the restrictions as to eligibility as the minister has detailed them here, and while I am unable to pass any comment on the validity of the amendments it would seem to us none the less that they appear on their face to be of the kind that should be approved by the house. Because of that we will be happy to see the bill receive second reading and sent to the committee on veterans affairs, so that it may be considered by that committee.
Meanwhile I wonder if the minister could say at this stage how much higher than the estimates are the number of children receiving educational assistance under the act? He said the figures were higher than those estimated when the act was introduced and he thought that was all to the good, with which I think I would agree. I wonder if when the time comes to reply the minister would give those figures at this stage.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ALLOWANCE AND EXTEND BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure there is complete unanimity in the committee on the amendments proposed by the minister in this resolution. I was interested when he mentioned the fact that the number who were eligible was somewhat higher than was expected. I am pleased to hear that, and to learn that the act has been of benefit to a larger number than we expected.
I notice that there are two amendments. One extends the eligibility to include certain groups presently excluded, as explained by the minister, and we are pleased to support that proposal. The second amendment provides for the payment of an allowance of $60 per month which, if I understood the minister correctly, is the same amount paid to student veterans.
I am keen on this act because I know of a number of cases of children of deceased veterans in my constituency who have benefited from this act, and I want to emphasize the following remarks. When we can spend millions of dollars to bring certain immigrants to this country, and in some cases spend good Canadian dollars to bring and maintain immigrants here for a year who have fought against us, there should not be a single disabled veteran in this country suffer on any account because of the failure of this government to provide for his needs. Second, there should not be a single veteran's dependant in this country suffer on any account whatever or because of the failure of this government to provide for his or her needs. And third, and of equal importance, there should not be a single child of a deceased veteran who has

fought in defence of his country and of freedom denied the opportunity of receiving an education.
Therefore on behalf of this group I want to express the strongest support possible for this act and for the amendments, and we trust it will be further amended to meet the representations of the Canadian Legion when that day arrives.

That number is 507. I might add that under the new amendments we anticipate the number receiving benefits will be in the neighbourhood of between 720 and 740.
I wish to thank the hon. member for Kootenay-West for his co-operation, which I have always received in the past. He mentioned the spending of considerable sums of money for bringing immigrants to this country. I would merely point out to him that this country has been settled by immigrants. As I read over the list of names of those who have received benefits under this act I observe that many of them are children of immigrants who came to Canada and served Canada in the last war. So those who came to our shores may be immigrants today but they will be Canadians tomorrow, and we find that in the past the immigrants and their children have played a significant role in the building up of this country and will do so in the future.

Mr. Chairman, with the permission of the committee I should like to revert to a matter which was under discussion yesterday, namely the dismissal of one Walter Mitchell, formerly employed as a checker and fumigator in the port of Montreal. I shall try to discuss this case without acrimony and as quietly and equitably as I can having regard to the circumstances.
The question arose some time ago because of a starred question which I put on the order paper. It also came up during a short discussion of the estimates of the Department of Agriculture one day last week and again yesterday when I moved to have certain documents produced in connection with the dismissal. I would have thought the minister would have had no objection to the production of these documents, because when a person is dismissed and loses his employment there should be no objection on the part of those taking such action to producing the evidence upon which the dismissal is based. For those reasons I should now like to put on record the other side of the case.
Mr. Walter Mitchell was a checker and fumigator at the port of Montreal for the last 22 years. I have forgotten how many years the minister said he was employed, not that long, but the information I have in my possession is that he has been employed in that capacity perhaps not during all the time but certainly in the Department of Agriculture for 22 years. He was employed during the season of navigation only; that is, he began his work in April and terminated it in December. He was a loyal, efficient, assiduous and honest employee of the Department of Agriculture. In fact, I am informed that

Supply-A griculture
heard and contrary, I say again, to the resolution approved by both parties in this house over the years.
The only way, as I say, in which this man could have been dismissed was either by the certificate of a member of parliament or by an investigation made by an impartial tribunal. In essence an individual should not be dismissed under any circumstances without being given the opportunity of being heard. The principle is clear. It is based upon the assumption that an hon. member of this house who certifies to such a condition has satisfied himself to his own personal knowledge as to the authenticity of the statements he makes, and that they are true; but if he makes such a statement without regard to the fine detail of it being true or untrue and the individual is dismissed, I think the man probably has an action against the member of parliament because he has compassed his dismissal and destroyed his position.
These were the reasons why, after a lengthy debate, the conclusion was arrived at that this was the only fair, equitable and reasonable manner in which to dispense with the services of an individual. Therefore with regard to the political activity part of this case I conclude that the man, Walter Mitchell, has not been dismissed in accordance with the long standing practice of the house and that a grave and serious injustice has been done to him under the circumstances.
The next reason given by the minister was that Walter Mitchell was in possession of contraband liquor and contraband cigarettes. What are the facts? I hold in my hand a document which the minister refused to produce yesterday. It is from the Department of National Revenue, customs and excise division, and is dated December 23, 1957, almost a full month after the alleged charge against Mr. Mitchell, which offence was said to have occurred on November 29, 1957. It is the usual and very ordinary notice served pursuant to sections 158 to 166 of the Customs Act advising this man that he was in possession of five bottles of liquor and six cartons of cigarettes. What member of parliament who has been in the house for any length of time has not acted on behalf of constituents who have brought such notices to him because they have been searched by a customs officer and found in possession of cigarettes or other articles they have brought into Canada without payment of the excise tax?
Over the many years I have been here I have had many such notices brought to me. Many of them were of little or no importance. Others were more serious and still others were very serious. But the point I

wish to make is that this was not a charge but a notice pursuant to sections 158 to 166 of the Customs Act to the effect that Mitchell had in his possession liquor and cigarettes upon which the excise tax had not been paid. It was not considered serious by departmental officers. Revenue officers came to his home. He opened the door and said, "Look at the premises; you are entirely welcome to find what there is here." He told them how these articles came into his possession and he invited them to confirm the information he gave them. They must have done so, because a little later he received a notice from the same department, pursuant to sections 158 to 166 of the Customs Act, to the effect that the statements he had made were found to be true and that the officers of the Department of National Revenue were not proceeding against him.
I do not have that letter. I had hoped to get it from the minister when I moved for the production of papers. I was not able to get it. I have therefore only the information which has been brought to my attention; but the information is that the letter was forthcoming and did go to Mitchell to indicate that the department had no intention of proceeding because they did not consider this matter as being of a serious nature. If that is the case, I think the minister did the house an injustice when he did not produce that information. Notwithstanding that, I now hold in my hand two documents from officers of the Department of Agriculture attesting to the fact that Mitchell was a good, honest and assiduous worker.

I the undersigned do hereby solemnly declare, that for the past twelve years, acting in the capacity of supervisor of checkers and fumigators for the port of Montreal, that Mr. W. P. Mitchell was employed under my supervision, and has always been punctual, courteous, sober, reliable, rendered valuable service, and has always reported and remained on duty when requested.
J. J. Kieran
Sworn before me at Montreal, Que. this 20th day of June, 1958.

This statement comes many months after it is alleged by the minister that Mr. Mitchell was found in possession of contraband liquor. Surely the official, his own official, must have known about this alleged offence and he could not have considered it serious when he, in the face of these facts, gave the statement which I have put on the record.
Then from a higher official of the Department of Agriculture, namely Dr. G. T. Labelle, regional veterinarian for the city of Montreal, comes this statement which is in French and which I shall read and translate. It is dated June 19, 1958:
A Qui de droit.
Ceci est pour attester que Monsieur Walter Mitchell, durant son emploi k notre Minister e comme Verificateur et Fumigateur, a toujours 6t6 ponctuel et assidu k son travail. Nous n'avons aucun reproche k lui adresser concernant l'accom-plissement de ses devoirs.
This statement translated in my best English is as follows:
To whom it may concern:
This is to certify that Mr. Walter Mitchell during his employment in our department as a checker and fumigator was always punctual and assiduous at his work. We have no blame or reproach to attach to him concerning the accomplishment of his duties.
This is dated June 19, many months-in facts five or six months-after this alleged offence. Furthermore, notwithstanding that the minister said on two occasions that this man had been guilty of an offence on November 29, 1957, he was called back to work in April, 1958. If this charge was so serious and if it had not been abandoned, as I am informed, why was he called back to work? I have put on the record what the facts are.
I say to the minister that he has dealt unfairly and unjustly with this man. I say furthermore that he has maligned this man's reputation by putting on the record a statement which is certainly not in accordance with what he said the other day and with the facts. He has clearly left himself open also to an action for defamation of character if made outside the house. He has dismissed a person who was in the employ of his department for 22 years, and he refuses to produce the evidence. He says he has affidavits and photographs, but he does not want to give them to the house. He guarantees that the facts are accurate, but he will not tell us on what he bases his judgment. He says he decided not to prosecute because he did not want to give the case any publicity.
May I say that the case was not one in his department. The case came from another department, if there was a case; and there was no prosecution. The minister had nothing to do with the matter in so far as the other department was concerned.
Supply-Agriculture
The minister said he knew about this case only two or three months before July 23, which was when he spoke. If he knew about it only then, how could he refuse to prosecute as he said he did? Then of course he went on to say that he did not like the questions that were being asked. He decided this matter without inquiry and without investigation. When a man makes his livelihood by means of a position such as the one held by this man, and when he has been discharging his duty over the years-for 22 years in this case-without the slightest complaint and with the strongest recommendations even after the alleged infraction, I say that his reputation is at stake when action of the kind taken by the minister has been taken.
The decision of the minister was taken ex parte. I say again that he has committed a grave injustice to Walter Mitchell, particularly as this action comes from a minister of a government pledged to bring down a bill on civil rights by which the rights of the individual are to be protected. The rights of the individual in this case are clearly established by the record and the practice and procedure over the years in this house. That practice has not been followed. Someone in the department, evidently of a different political faith from that of Mr. Mitchell, has reported against him.
While it was the minister's prerogative to accept the report and consider it, I say that he should not have acted upon it (1) without getting a certificate from a member of parliament or (2) without conducting an investigation. An investigation was not conducted. The minister proceeded without an inquiry. I submit that his action is contrary to the practice; the rules of this house and contrary to justice. In the name of justice I demand that an investigation be now held into this case by an impartial tribunal.

Mr. Chairman, I feel that the opposition has caused enough waste of time as it is and that the house had better come back to the subject of the debate, that is, agriculture. May I therefore point out that, in the few months during which the Conservative party has been managing the affairs of this country, it has, in this very short time, brought in much legislation which, certainly, has been most useful to the farmers of this country.
Thanks to the Conservative party's progressive policy, farm revenue keeps growing. For the first quarter of 1958, farm income has reached $604 million, an increase of $29 million over that of the same period in 1957. This increase, Mr. Chairman, is mainly due to increased production and higher prices paid for cattle.
Since 1953, the number of Canadian farmers has dropped 10 per cent. Under the administration of our hon. friends in the opposition, production costs were rising and prices were on the down grade. Between 1946 and 1956, the prices of commodities and services to Canadian farmers have gone up 58.2 per cent, while farm products rose by only 1.7 per cent.
From 1951 to 1956, the prices of commodities and services to the farmers rose by 5.5 per cent and the price of their products decreased by 21.8 per cent.

As to the province of Quebec-still from the farming angle-may I be allowed to point out, Mr. Chairman, that over 88 per cent of Quebec farms now use electricity.

If the hon. member for Drum-mond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger), the would-be minister of agriculture, who never will be such in any case, wishes to take the floor, he may do so after I am through.
Mr. Chairman, some years ago, the federal government granted subsidies to those who wanted to exchange their sap buckets. That policy lasted for 15 years, from 1940 to 1955. As a result, in the province of Quebec, about 18 million sap buckets were exchanged.
I am wondering, Mr. Chairman, why the previous government discontinued that policy which favoured the agricultural class of the province of Quebec, when it is also well known that the federal government, through an act of parliament, forbids any traces of lead in maple products. The UCC, and several other farm organizations, had asked the former government to carry on this policy of sap bucket exchange, but the former government nonetheless discontinued this policy, probably because the province of Quebec was supporting a Liberal government.
But this situation will now cease. We have in the person of the hon. Minister of Agriculture a man who is close to the average Canadian, and to the farmer. It will not take 22 years, Mr. Chairman, for the agricultural class to benefit from the advantages of this government's policy. Mr. Chairman, I urge the government to consider the possibility of restoring this policy of sap bucket exchange. Cost to the government would be about $50,000 a year.
Mr. Chairman, I know that the hon. Minister for Agriculture is now studying the possibility of devising some crop insurance program, to help all Canadian farmers engaged in mixed farming. Crop insurance
[Mr. Pigeon.l
legislation of this type has been in force in the United States for over 20 years. We have begun to hear about it since the Conservative government is in power. How is it, Mr. Chairman, that our friends of the opposition, who claimed to be the friends of the ordinary Canadian, never brought up the subject of crop insurance, or never as much as hinted that farmers might have it some time? I know that the hon. Minister of Agriculture is considering the possibility of developing a crop insurance program, and I might say to the would-be minister of agriculture from the opposition, the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska, that it will not take 22 years for such a program to be applied in the various provinces of Canada.
I urge the Minister of Agriculture to introduce crop insurance legislation, and I would advise him also to consider the possibility of applying such legislation, first of all, to specialized farming such as, for instance, the growing of pipe, cigar and cigarette tobacco, since such crops are very important, not only in my constituency, but also in Ontario.
Do you know how much it costs a Quebec farmer to set up a cigarette tobacco-growing farm? He must first of all pay $50,000 and, each year afterwards, he has to spend nearly $10,000 on labour, fertilizers and all sorts of services, to obtain a good crop.
Quebec tobacco growers, and those of Ontario too, feel they are entitled to crop insurance legislation. They are anxious that such legislation be put into force. That is why I would ask the Minister of Agriculture to consider the possibility of applying such legislation first of all to specialized farming, even if it has to be improved afterwards, and extend it as far as possible to other crops, all over the country.
Well, Mr. Chairman, each year, in the federal constituency of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, considerable damage is caused by hail or frost, with attendant loss of farm income. Only recently, farmers of my constituency came up to me and said that hail had wrought havoc in their cigar tobacco fields at St. Esprit, St. Lin and St. Roch-West, in the county of Assomption and that of Montcalm.
Crop insurance is essential to the future and success of the farmers of this country. Before putting in his crop, the farmer needs to have some idea of the price he will receive for his commodity, but he also needs protection

against hail, drought, wind and frost. The farmer has to be in exactly the same position as the worker who, before taking up a new job, inquires about the wages he will get and asks $1.50, $2.00 or $3.00 an hour, according to his trade. Before starting on a job, he finds out how much he will get out of it, before trading his skill for a wage.
Likewise before a farmer begins working his land or putting money and labour into it he must be assured of a profit from what will grow out of his land. I know that the Minister of Agriculture, in co-operation with the government, has made extensive studies into the possibility of implementing steps to the benefit of the farmers of this country. Crop insurance is absolutely essential to the future of specialized farming and of Canadian agriculture in general.
Mr. Chairman, I know that the Minister of Agriculture, more than anybody else, is concerned with the needs of the farmer and has made very careful study of that legislation. The member for Drummond-Arthabaska, pseudo-minister of agriculture-who in any event will never be minister of agriculture -would like this government to bring in within the space of a few weeks or a few months all those measures which his party failed to introduce during the 22 years they were in power, in spite of the representations of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, for instance, or of farm groups in the province of Quebec or elsewhere in Canada. Instead, his party chose to ignore the needs of the people, and preferred to use closure rather than take heed of the needs of the farmers of the province of Quebec, and of the country.
Mr. Chairman, I am also happy to note that the Minister of Agriculture is proceeding to put an effective end to dumping of American farm produce. I know that one New England senator at least has stated that Canadians had some reason to be annoyed at the United States and asked that more attention be henceforth directed to economic policy so as to contribute to the improvement of relations between the two countries. Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Agriculture-and this did not take 22 years-has already started putting a stop to dumping of farm commodities from the United States, a thing which our opponent's administration had never managed to do. What was done to attain these results? Well, the Conservative government has imposed a customs duty of 13i cents per pound on American strawberries.

The Conservative government has also prevented dumping of American cheddar cheese. Severe restrictions were enacted with regard to the import of skim milk powder from the United States or New Zealand. I hope the Minister of Agriculture will continue along those lines. This does not mean that we will be persecuting the Americans.
May I be allowed at this point to quote an example of what happened on the Montreal market. Right in the middle of the production season, hundreds upon hundreds of carloads of vegetables from the United States were dumped on that market at the very moment our truck gardeners were attempting to market their produce on the same spot. This is also the case on the Toronto market and, indeed, when they arrive on this market with a truck full of vegetables, American farmers are just dumping their products here. I urge the Minister of Agriculture to pursue his action to stop that dumping. That doesn't mean that anyone should be persecuted, but we have to think of the average Canadian, that is the Canadian farmer. Just imagine: In a British Columbia camp the government of our opponents served United States potatoes to Hungarian refugees! That is how our farmers have been treated;-American potatoes served to Hungarian refugees.
That is what our opponents did to our Canadian farmers Mr. Chairman, and to-day they are defending the cause of our farmers in a tremulous voice, like an offended maiden. Well, they also served United States potatoes. ..

Mr. Chairman, the hon. minister of trade (Mr. Churchill) announced some time ago that the government, following some representations made by Canada, was going to allow more fresh apples to be exported to the United Kingdom than at the present time.
The new policy with regard to the exportation of fresh apples to the United Kingdom will give us a chance during July and the next eleven months, to sell 1,500,000 hundredweight of that farm product, i.e., 300,000 hundredweight from July to the end of December 1958, and 1,200,000 hundredweight from January to the end of June 1959.

Supply-Agriculture
The Conservative government had been in power only a few weeks or a few months when it began to reclaim this lost market. I might say in all sincerity and frankness that the English market is vital to us, as England imports about 60 per cent of its farm products from abroad. Let us help them get the necessary Canadian dollars, and, in return, Great Britain will buy our surpluses of wheat, eggs and dairy products.
I strongly urge the government to reclaim that market, Mr. Chairman. What happened during the war? The Liberal government rationed the Canadian people and sold to Great Britain our farm products like wheat, meat, eggs, milk, butter, cheese, apples, etc., at a rebate.
We had obtained by contract a privileged market in return for this sacrifice. Our hon. friends then in power lost the English market, the best farm market in the world. However, following a request from the Liberals, Canadians organized themselves in order to increase production, they capitalized in order to meet the needs of that privileged market. The government of the day has not been able to keep the English market for them so that they might export their farm surpluses there.
At one time, England bought Nova Scotia apples. Having lost the English market, the federal government granted subsidies so that our apple trees could be replaced by other crops. England, which used to buy its lumber in British Columbia, now buys it elsewhere. It is also getting its newsprint, its eggs, its dairy products, its wheat and its meat in other countries.
I strongly urge the hon. Minister of Agriculture to consider, in co-operation with the Minister of Trade, whether it might be possible to go further ahead with the sale of our Canadian apples in the United Kingdom. I trust that the apple growers of the province of Quebec and elsewhere in the country would rejoice in seeing such a policy applied.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to deal now with the experimental farm of l'Assomption. What happened in 1956? Discontinued was the agricultural information service, that of soils analysis, that of bacteriological analysis of milk, and of purebred dairy herds. I charge the government of the time with sabotaging that experimental farm. Farmers in my riding are dissatisfied with the way the experimental farm of l'Assomption was dealt

with. Yet, my riding is perhaps the largest dairy farming area in this country, being so close to the Montreal market. Dairying is its chief industry, followed by tobacco, poultry raising and truck farming. Under the former Liberal administration, the experimental farm of l'Assomption has been disorganized to a point where it no longer is able to give the important services it used to provide for the farmers and dairy producers of my constituency. The former administration has sabotaged the experimental farm of l'As-somption. The farmers have complained many times over about that behaviour of the former Liberal regime, but no one paid any attention to them. I urge the Minister of Agriculture to consider the possibility of reorganizing the experimental farm at l'As-somption. I also ask that the necessary grants be made to enable that farm to carry on the research needed to discover brands of tobacco which are milder than those the producers of my riding are now marketing.
A country can prosper only if its farmers prosper. As a rule farmers are heavy buyers of all sorts of goods, and they contribute to the wealth of the Canadian nation.
I want now to say a few words about the prices of farm machinery. I find the price of implements exceedingly high in relation to farmers' income.
The price of farm machinery has skyrocketed since the war.

In dealing with the agricultural situation as it exists today and looking forward to what we hope for in the years to come, one cannot help but look back to what has taken place in the years that have gone by. If we do that we cannot help but remember the men who have played an important part in the Canadian agricultural scene. All of us will recall the work of the late Hon. W. K. Motherwell who for many

years was minister of agriculture. As one who comes from the province of Saskatchewan I know that the people of that province appreciate the wonderful work that he did and although he was a member of the party that is in opposition today we feel that he continued the work begun in years gone by to build a better agricultural economy for Canada as a whole.

speechtext:
Following him, of course, came Robert Weir who in many respects was responsible for placing upon the statute books of the country much of the legislation that has endured to give agriculture those things that today are becoming even more important in our day to day living. One must also remember the Right Hon. James Garfield Gardiner, also a resident of the province of Saskatchewan. I have been surprised that members of the opposition have not referred to him very much in discussing agricultural matters but regardless of what they may think of him I want to say that he made a very notable contribution to the agriculture scene and, considering what he had to work with, I think he did a wonderful job.
I can pay tribute to him, to Mr. Motherwell and to Mr. Weir because today we have in the Minister of Agriculture a man who is following in the same tradition and placing upon the statute books of our country legislation that will give the farmers right across the country a little more security and stability than they have had in years gone by. We remember the improvements that were made by other governments and other parties but while they were and are good in themselves we say that they can be improved upon. I recall the prices support act brought in following the war which was supposed to be written in such a way to give to those engaged in agriculture a fair share of the national income. Well, we waited for a great number of years. I believe it took some 13 years for us to realize the extent of the fair share of the national income provided by that legislation as a result of the way in which it was interpreted. Because of this situation things happened in June of 1957 and again in March of this year. Farm people right across the country are looking to the government with a measure of expectation never before known as between the electors and a government.
I believe the reason they are looking to the government and to parliament is the legislation that was placed on the statute books 57071-3-184J
Supply*-Agriculture
in the last session of the House of Commons when Bill No. 237, having to do with the marketing of certain agricultural products, became the law of the land. This legislation, in the language in which it is written, gives to the agricultural industry those things that farmers and farm organizations have fought for and sought for more than 50 years. The notable exception, of course, is that it does not do anything for the people engaged in the growing of wheat, oats, barley and other grains in western Canada.
All members of the house know the record in that regard. All members know that representations were made by organizations in the province of Saskatchewan and elsewhere in western Canada that wheat, oats and barley should not be included under the act. In what I am about to say I am speaking for myself and not for the government. I think that the farm organizations made a mistake. I also think that the government made a mistake in listening to the farm organizations and not placing wheat, oats and barley under the price stabilization act. History alone will show whether that view is right or wrong. One thing is certain. Those who produce livestock products and other products covered by the legislation can look forward today with a little more confidence than at any time in the past.
I speak as a grain grower, one who knows what it was like to sell our product during years when people in other parts of Canada were enjoying an increasing measure of security and stability in their jobs, at a lower price than we should have received because of regulations enacted by the parliament of the country. I think too of the years following when the price of our product gradually dropped while the price of everything that went into the production of the product kept on rising. On this occasion I cannot help but remind the Minister of Agriculture and the other ministers on the treasury benches, as the people of western Canada do not need to be reminded, that the grain growers are in a desperate situation today, a situation brought about not by an administration that lasted for one, two, three or four years but by an administration that over many years failed to face the problems associated with the production of this commodity which has made Canada known all over the world as the home of the finest protein wheat that people can buy. The people of the world choose Canadian wheat if they have the money to buy it. Other countries have subsidized their agricultural industries in an effort to make themselves self-sufficient but still require some of the wheat we grow in western Canada. Despite that fact we saw

Supply-A griculture session after session go by with nothing being done by a party that said it stood for the farm people of the country, that it stood for agriculture and free trade, a party that said it was guaranteeing our farmers a fair share of the national income and whose minister of agriculture came from the province of Saskatchewan, the greatest grain producing area in Canada. Yet they allowed that industry to sink to the depths that it reached a year ago and is still in today.
During the election campaign the leader of the Liberal party, who is Leader of the Opposition in the house, had occasion to come to Rosthern constituency to deal with agricultural policy and at that time he had certain things to say. I dealt with some of them the other night when the question of deficiency payments was brought up and I am not going to repeat what I said then. But I have a press report of his speech here and among the many things he had to say he said this:
We propose to raise the initial price of oats to farmers from 60 to 65 cents per bushel for No. 2 G.W., in store Fort William; and the initial price of barley from 96 cents to $1.00 per bushel basis No. 3 C'W. in store Fort William.
When the people of my constituency heard that they said that if any one should increase the price of oats by five cents per bushel it was the party that had reduced the price by five cents at a time when farm costs in western Canada were rising as they had never risen before. But the interesting thing is. that he went on to say:
These increases would be promptly reflected in increased payments to farmers. They would not, however, add to the cost of feed grain to livestock producers in any part of Canada.
In one breath he was going to raise the price five cents. In another breath it was not going to cost anyone any more money. That is about as empty a promise as I ever heard during any election campaign in any part of this country. There was really one interesting thing he had to say and it was this and I quote:
The traditional or historical pattern of low incomes of most farmers has made for poor housing -far below urban standards.
I should like to emphasize that statement. What a statement that was to come from a member of a cabinet that on three occasions at least came to the farm people of this country with the slogan "You never had it better", then we find the statement being made that the traditional or historical pattern of low incomes of most farmers has made for poor housing far below urban standards. We have that statement coming from the Leader of the Opposition, the leader of a party that has appealed to the people on those terms and

has said that their agricultural support program was based on those principles which would assure to the people of Canada in agriculture their fair share of the national income. Then he says that the traditional or historical pattern of low incomes of most farmers has made for poor housing.
I just wanted to read that into the record because, after all, Mr. Chairman, we hear a great deal about the promises that have been made and the promises that have not been made. But above all these things we know that whoever is in power, whoever is charged with responsibility of the Minister of Agriculture tries to do his best for the people of this country. All I want to say is that if that was the best that the Liberal party could do, it was surely time that we had a change of government here in Canada and gave someone else a chance to try to do better.
In so far as Bill No. 237 is concerned, may I say that I have heard people in the house here say that it is not giving to some producers what they had expected. All I want to say about it is that I believe the people of my constituency are willing to give the bill a chance to work and are willing to give this government and the Minister of Agriculture and also the Minister of Finance a chance to feel their way in order to find out what measure of support they can justifiably give to the people engaged in this most important segment of our industry.
In passing from Bill No. 237 I should like to say that I think it is an improvement over the old legislation. If anything detrimental can be said with regard to what has taken place so far under the bill, the only thing I can say about it is that we have not had wheat, oats and barley under it. While that is my personal opinion, it is an opinion not shared by some of the people in agriculture in western Canada. However, it is still my opinion and I wanted to get it put on the record today.
During this session we have noted many amendments to existing legislation dealing with agriculture and the problems of farmers right across Canada. What I like is the national approach that this government is taking to the many problems affecting this important industry. For the first time people in all parts of Canada can come to the government and, upon the basis of what is taking place in other parts of the country, justify their demands for like treatment. That is something that has been wanting in the administration of the Department of Agriculture for many years.
We have seen the development of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act in western Canada. Some amendments made this year may

solve some of the problems. 1 think they will possibly solve many of them. However, in the application of them I think it may be found that one or two things were overlooked, although not intentionally.
There is another part of the agricultural policy to which I wish to make reference, namely the freight assistance policy on grains moved from western Canada to feeders in eastern Canada. I have heard some people say that that is a subsidy to the western Canadian farmer. The western Canadian farmer figures that it is a subsidy to the eastern feeder. I am not going to try to say who is right and who is wrong in the matter. All I am going to say is that it is a policy for the moving of grain from the west to the east and also to round out a little bit sounder agricultural policy for Canada and for Canadians.
The board of grain commissioners handle the grain act in this country. I think it is a tribute to all who have been associated with that department that we have been able to establish ourselves in the world markets with a name in so far as the quality of our grain is concerned. All of us who produce grain in western Canada like to haggle with the elevator agent about grades, weight, dockage and all of these other things but every one of us is proud of what has been set up and has given us a chance to enjoy our share of the world market for this important commodity that perhaps is more powerful than any other single thing used by people in any part of the world. When I think of that, I cannot help but think-

Mr. Chairman, at six o'clock I was dealing, among other things, with the growth of a national agricultural policy in Canada which would give to all our farm people equal recognition. I went on to commend the present government and particularly the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Agriculture for the part they have played in pursuing this objective, but there is another minister of the crown, namely the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who constantly bears in mind the people engaged in our agricultural industry. Trade and agriculture are complementary to each other, and I do not wish to turn the minister's head but
Supply-Agriculture
I would like to say I think he has done a notable job during the last several months in increasing the sales of western grain, particularly wheat. This also applies of course to grain sales in eastern Canada.
I have already mentioned the amendments passed by this house and I did not name them singly, because that would take too long. The problems in respect to agriculture all across this country do not differ very much. We all share, wherever we farm in Canada, the need for improved credit facilities. We all share in the benefits of increased markets for our products and the benefits accruing from legislation introduced to take care of disasters from time to time. We all share in the benefits of a proper price relationship between our goods and those of other industries and I have in mind particularly cereal grains, potatoes and fishing industry, which are the most important industries presenting problems to us at the present time.
These industries still appear to require the attention of the government with respect to some definite legislation, and I would suggest to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and to his department that at the Brussels fair Canadian fish and chips might be served and a bun made of good Canadian grain might be thrown in for good measure. Such a scheme might do something to develop interest in Canadian products. The minister might make a note of that suggestion because I may ask a question one of these days in order to discover whether those items have in fact been served at the Brussels exhibit.
In regard to the credit situation I notice that some members, particularly those in the C.C.F. group, have maintained that what we require is credit available for a 40-year period. In this connection I would point out that other workers expect to retire after a period of 20 to 25 years, during which time they hope to build up a pension in order to make this possible. I think, therefore, it is stretching it a little too far to say that if you agree other labour groups should be able to retire in 20 to 25 years that you expect at the same time the agricultural workers will be labouring under conditions which will prevent them from paying back the mortgages on their farms in less than 40 years. After all, the farm people are entitled to the same things to which others are entitled and I think, therefore, that a 25-year term would be a sufficient length of time to set for a farm mortgage. Why should we want the farmer to retire and have to hand over to his sons and daughters a heritage of a 15-year mortgage?
Another aspect of the matter with which I would like to deal is a possibility of something which might happen on a farm-I do

Supply-Agriculture
not think it will happen in Canada but there is always the possibility. I have in mind that some day the Canadian farm loan board under such a set-up as has been suggested would acquire the bulk of our agricultural land and no matter from what province a farmer may come, I do not think he would want to think that at some time in the future he would be able to secure land only on a lease basis.
The first responsibility of any government is to build a national program which will eliminate inequities such as those which plague certain sectors of our economy from time to time. The second responsibility as I see it is to ensure some measure of assistance to those sectors in case of disaster which, because of national trends and policies, might mean that certain districts might find themselves in great difficulty and be unable to continue as effective and efficient productive areas.
The people in agriculture today are well informed, generally speaking, and one cannot place before them a proposition based on a false premise. They know the prices exacted by industry, labour and capital in the national scene, no matter in what part of the country they may live, because they have to pay those prices in order to remain a working partner in the Canadian nation. That is why I urge upon this government, which has already set the pace, to continue towards the objective I have outlined of providing a fair share of the national income for agriculture.
The administrative branch of the Department of Agriculture has a notable tradition and like everything which is notable the passage of time has left some marks upon this tradition. One thing is certain and that is that this government will never go wrong if it continues to build upon the foundations which have been laid legislation designed to complete a truly national policy for our country, one which will strengthen Canada from coast to coast and, what is more, will encourage and exemplify that spirit and understanding of freedom, that love of the soil, which constitutes the way of life in the Canadian agricultural industry.
I was in the reading room this evening and I noticed an article in the Star-Phoenix of July 26, which referred to Dr. B. M. Craig of the prairie regional laboratory of the national research council. He speaks of the strides that are being made to make rapeseed available for use in margarine. We know today that many of the firms in eastern Canada are exhibiting quite an interest in this subject and I merely wish to say that the research program undertaken by the Department of Agriculture is one of the most important services being rendered to Canada.

It is important not only to the farm people but to every consumer because every stride forward in connection with new varieties, increased yields and advances along those lines, benefit every person in this country.
I am not going to say anything further because like all other members I would like to get on with the job of going through these estimates and I hope we will soon get back to our constituencies so that we may meet the people who produce these goods.
