speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the debate on the first item of the estimates of the Department of Agriculture was adjourned on Friday, July 11 at five o'clock in order to revert to private and public bills, I had just stated that the prices received by small farmers for pulpwood was far from satisfactory and barely met the cost of cutting this pulpwood and taking it to the roadside. I had also placed on record the statement by the Prime Minister, as reported in the Toronto Star of February 27, 1958, which was made in Summerside, P.E.I. where the Prime Minister had said that he hoped the advisory committee and the stabilization board would give consideration to including farm produced wood in the provisions of the act so that farmers would know for at least a year in advance the lowest price they would receive.
This evening I have another statement which was made by the Prime Minister in Charlottetown, P.E.I., and I wish to place this statement on record. I hope the Prime Minister is listening on the other end of the line and will come rushing in to confirm or reject this statement. The statement, as reported in the Toronto Star of February 28 reads as follows:
Mr. Diefenbaker . . . gave audiences at Charlottetown and Summerside an interpretation of the Agricultural Price Stabilization Act which would come as news to members of parliament.
"The day will never come in Canada, no matter how great the crash (in agricultural prices) in other countries, that prices will fall to the same

level here," he asserted. "There is a distress price in Canada below which all agricultural prices cannot fall," he said at Summerside.
The Prime Minister maintained here and at Summerside that there was a provision in the bill to provide a minimum support price "under all agricultural products" of 80 per cent of the price over the previous 10 years.
The act introduced in parliament by the Conservative government last year appeared to provide this protection by statute for only nine agricultural products-butter, eggs, cheese, hogs, sheep, cattle and non-prairie produced wheat, oats and barley.
Parliament was certainly never given the impression that the legislation would provide protection for all the commodities produced by the farmer in the event of the bottom falling out of the world market.
Last night, the Prime Minister charged the opposition parties with misrepresenting the Conservative farm bill. On the face of it, he appears to have been guilty of misrepresentation on his own account.
Yesterday at Rimouski, speaking of the same bill, Mr. Diefenbaker hinted that pulpwood cut by farmers might be eligible for price supports. Last night he indicated that producers of potatoes a major crop here, might also apply to the price stabilization board to have supports put under that crop.
Now this statement was made by the Prime Minister over five months ago and our farmers are still waiting for pulpwood to be placed under price support.
On May 28 the hon. member for Drum-mond-Arthabaska asked the Minister of Agriculture the following question as reported in Hansard at page 580:
Mr. Speaker, will the Minister of Agriculture advise the house if it is the intention of the government to establish floor prices on maple sugar and pulpwood.
He received the following answer from the Minister of Agriculture:
In so far as maple sugar is concerned, I replied to a similar question last week, and the hon. member will find the answer in Hansard. In so far as pulpwood is concerned, we are giving some consideration to that matter but to date we have made no decision.
Two months have passed since then, and no decision has yet been taken by the department or by the prices support board in this regard. Our small farmers in eastern Canada depend largely on the sale of pulpwood from their own wood lots for ready cash to meet their obligations, and it is important that they be given the same advantages as are being offered to producers of other farm products throughout the country.
When a farmer is being paid as low as $8.50 for rough pulp out of his own wood lot, as was paid in some of the eastern provinces last winter, there is something wrong somewhere and the government must intervene to remedy such conditions. We have all heard those words "disastrous floor prices for agricultural products which should not exist in our country". I know of no price which is
Supply-Agriculture
more disastrous than the one being paid our small farmers for the pulpwood cut from their own wood lots.
Another problem which seriously affects the operations of our small farm owners is the financing necessary to ensure that these family farms are preserved intact. The application of the farm loan board regulations has not been of too valuable assistance to our small farm owners. The last report published a few weeks ago shows that out of $69 million made available as loans in the last fiscal year, only $680,000, less than 1 one per cent, went to the province of New Brunswick. Loans to small farmers have been difficult to obtain and on many occasions our farmers were told that it was useless for them to even apply. The establishment of a farm loan bank would facilitate loans to farmers and make it possible for them to purchase land, to obtain equipment and to make their farm operations worth while.
Such a plan would certainly extend the borrowing facilities now available through the farm loan board. It would assist young Canadians to establish themselves on land, thus enabling them to take full advantage of the opportunities available to our farming population.
The establishment of a farm loan bank, operating under regulations somewhat similar to those of the industrial development bank, with agencies in every province and with lending facilities extending to individual farmers and fishermen would be a great advantage to the farm population of this country and to our fishermen. Such a farm loan bank, or even proper amendments to the National Housing Act, could also provide loans to young farmers to build new homes. I know I should be out of order if I began to speak about the need for housing in rural areas at this point, but I would urge the minister to have a special survey made in this regard with reference to the need of better homes for farmers. Our small farmers in eastern Canada need new homes, new buildings and better equipment. Our farmers cannot finance such improvements on their own, and it is the duty of the government to make adequate provision for such financing.
On Friday, July 11, in the course of my remarks, I mentioned that we from the maritime provinces wanted to know why potatoes were not included on the permanent list of commodities coming under the Agricultural Prices Stabilization Act or, alternatively, we wanted a firm statement of policy from the government with regard to potatoes. Interjecting in these remarks, as

Supply-Agriculture
reported at page 2174 of Hansard of July 11, the Minister of Agriculture said:
They have had a great deal of protection; a lot of money has been paid out to them.
The minister referred, of course, to the potato producers. On different occasions during the present session we have heard hon. members on the government side of the house criticize the previous administration for not doing anything for the farmers. It may be well for them to know that in the last 20 years over $2| billion has been paid out of the federal treasury to the farmers of Canada. This evening I should like to place on the record what has been done by the previous administration for the potato farmers of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. Potatoes were supported under the Agricultural Prices Support Act for the crop years 1946, 1948, 1950, 1955 and 1956 previous to the support given in 1957. In addition, potatoes have come under the Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act which act is basically not designed for support but payments were made which had the effect of providing some support in connection with the 1950 and 1953 crops.
For example, the 1946 program indicates that potatoes delivered for processing bore a guaranteed price of $1.65 per barrel at factory for Canada No. 1 grade. Potatoes delivered for export or other shipment bore a price of $1 per 75 pound bag on car at shipping point bagged, tagged and inspected. The total cost of this program to the government was $170,748.48.
Under the 1948 program potatoes bore a price of $1.15 per 100 pounds in bulk on the grower's farm. The total cost of this program to the government was $1,646,739.34.
Under the 1950 program potatoes bore a guarantee of 60 cents per barrel when delivered under the Agricultural Products Cooperative Marketing Act guarantee, which guarantee also amounted to 60 cents per barrel. The total cost to the government of the support of 60 cents per barrel amounted to $218,687.79. The cost under the co-operative marketing act was approximately $50,000.
In 1953, under the Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act the government guaranteed an initial advance of 45 cents, 50 cents and 55 cents per bushel in Prince Edward Island and 40 cents, 45 cents and 55 cents per bushel in New Brunswick for different time periods. The total loss under this program was approximately $5 million.
The 1955 program consisted of the payment of $1 per barrel of 165 pounds for potatoes delivered to starch plants less whatever the government could recover from

the starch plants. The total government cost of this program was $4,830.77.
In 1956, under the program followed in that year, the support price was based on $1.65 per barrel provided the consumer market remained at a price of three-quarters of a cent per pound or higher on the average up to June 15. This was based on potatoes delivered for processing, with the government to pay the difference up to the figure of $1.65. The total cost of this program to the government was $449,279.16. As these figures will show, the previous administration certainly looked after the interests of the potato farmer.
What has been done this year by the present government for the potato growers of Prince Edward Island? We learned in this house that an application was made on May 16 by the potato growers of Prince Edward Island for assistance from the agricultural prices support board. The official offer by the federal government, or the confirmation of an offer, was made on June 24. On July 18 I directed a question to the Minister of Agriculture as reported at page 2364 of Hansard of that date in the following words:
My question is based on a press report in the Charlottetown Guardian of July 12 concerning price supports for potatoes, to the effect that all hope of receiving aid had vanished in so far as island growers were concerned. What factors have prevented the application of the provisions of the agricultural prices stabilization legislation to this important class of agricultural producer?
The Minister of Agriculture replied to my question as follows:
Nothing has prevented it. As a matter of fact an offer was made by the stabilization board, which was approved by the cabinet, to the Prince Edward Island potato producers to give them support on the same basis as it has been given in New Brunswick as far as potatoes which are diverted to starch in that province are concerned. The potato association there accepted the offer but subsequently discovered that the potatoes had sprouted to some extent and therefore there was difficulty in so far as determining the grade was concerned. We are carrying on further discussions at the present time to try to overcome this difficulty.
I asked a further question in these words:
May I ask as a supplementary question whether the delay of the government in applying this measure is not an example of the weakness of the agricultural stabilization program?
The Minister of Agriculture replied:
Mr. Speaker, since this statement has been made I think I should have the opportunity of answering it. Any delays which have taken place in regard to the potato situation in Prince Edward Island have been due to the provincial government and/or the potato association in that province not being able to make up their minds, not accepting the offer when it was made to them, and not putting the plan which was offered to them into operation.

The reply made by the minister was not exactly according to the facts and in it he placed the blame on the government of Prince Edward Island and the potato growers there.
I have in my hand an excerpt from the Charlottetown Guardian of July 12, 1958, which I wish to place on the record. It bears the title "Department Ruling Kills Potato Support Program" with the subtitle "Ottawa Refuses to Relax Regulations on Firmness" and it reads as follows:
Even while producers' applications for assistance under the prices support program continued to pile up in the office of the potato marketing board yesterday, official word came through from Ottawa that virtually all hope of receiving aid had vanished in so far as island growers are concerned.
William MacLennan, chairman of the potato marketing board, stated yesterday evening that L. W. Pearsall, chairman of the agricultural stabilization board informed him that no relaxation in the quality of Canada No. 1 grade potatoes could be entertained. Mr. Pearsall said he was making his statement after consultation with federal Minister of Agriculture, Douglas Harkness.
Further on the article states:
The potato board was conscious of the fact that very few island potatoes would qualify as Canada No. 1 in so far as firmness was concerned and informed Mr. Pearsall accordingly. Mr. Pearsall told the potato board that he was sending Mr. Eardley to the island "with the purpose of making the plan work".
Yesterday Mr. Eardley denied that he had come here to "make the plan work". He said he was merely a fact finding committee of one to appraise and report on the situation as he found it.
Further along the article reads:
Mr. MacLennan said the industry felt that the offer was not satisfactory either from a monetary standpoint or from a quality restriction angle. "However", he said, "we were forced to accept it with the hope that some of the restrictions would be lifted. The matter has now been finalized and we know where we stand."
Mr. MacLennan estimates that by the rate applications are reaching the potato board office it would appear that about 600 carloads remain unsold.
He said every effort to move the potatoes has been made.
As we can see from this report, the fault was not with the potato growers of Prince Edward Island, nor with the provincial government of the island; the fault was that the offer made by the federal government was not acceptable and would cover only about 15 per cent of the potatoes which were then available for sale.
I have a letter from a Prince Edward Island farmer which also appeared in the Charlottetown Guardian on Monday, July 14, 1958, and I feel that this letter should be placed on record to show the attitude of the Prince Edward Island farmers toward the offer which they received from the federal government. The letter reads as follows:
Supply-Agriculture
Sir:
May I have enough space in your column to say a word about the potato problem which is causing unprecedented consternation throughout the province at the present time.
For more than two months now, we in the potato industry have been trying to get some satisfaction from the federal government at Ottawa which promised in the last election that the interests of our potato growers would be protected.
Our growers know by now that the assistance we have been offered is completely worthless. Many of the growers, including myself, are caught with large quantities of potatoes still unsold. And the assistance that has been offered has been made worthless because of the restrictions.
Can you imagine, Mr. Editor, how anyone would expect a bin of potatoes to pass Canada No. 1 right now. None of them will. Yet the government at Ottawa refuses to consider our potatoes unless they do.
Three of our Conservative members are in the province today and I suggest it is their problem. They told us glibly and emphatically at election time that their government and its legislation would look after such an emergency. The emergency is here now and they are doing nothing about loosening the grave restrictions.
The way I see it is either one thing or the other. These members must fight for us and get our just desserts or else they had better resign and let someone else take over the job who may be able to serve us efficiently.
Fellow potato farmers I suggest you see your member today and impress this upon him. I have already seen mine.
Their leader, Mr. Diefenbaker, is the man who made the promises right here in this province that our potato crop would be protected under such an emergency. Now is the time for our members to see that Mr. Diefenbaker keeps his promise.
I am glad to see the Prime Minister now in his seat. I see the line is working. I continue:
At that time Mr. Diefenbaker was all for the farmer. At least that is what he told us. Now his government orders two potato inspectors to inspect a potato bin and warns them that two more will follow. Does this look as though it is the farmer he wants to help.
Those same inspectors were capable of inspecting potatoes to go to our best seed and table stock markets all over the world. But now when there is a chance to help the farmer, Mr. Diefenbaker wants four inspectors to do the job where growers with large holdings are concerned.
I am, sir, et cetera,
Neil Bradshaw,
Searletown.
There, Mr. Chairman, is the opinion of a farmer of the island on the help which was offered by the present government.

If my hon. friend only knew something about potatoes he would know that by the 26th day of June and early in July it is just not possible for the ordinary farmer to have all Canada No. 1 potatoes in

Supply-Agriculture
his potato bin. He is just showing his ignorance of the potato situation.
The statement which was made in this house on July 18 by the minister blaming the potato grower and the government of Prince Edward Island, was rightly challenged by Hon. Eugene Cullen, minister of agriculture for Prince Edward Island. Here again I have an article which appeared in the Guardian on July 19, and I feel that part of this article should be placed on the record of this house to challenge the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture. It reads:
Agriculture minister, Hon. Eugene Cullen, yesterday took strong exception to statements made by federal Minister of Agriculture, Douglas Harkness, in the House of Commons, regarding the implementation of a price support program for island potatoes.
Mr. Harkness was credited with saying "the delay in giving assistance to potato growers of P.E.I. was due to the growers themselves in not making up their minds whether to accept the government offer."
Mr. Harkness further stated that the plan offered to island growers was the same as that offered to New Brunswick growers in the starch diversion program. He concluded by placing all the blame on the government of Prince Edward Island and the growers in not deciding early whether to accept the offer.
In a prepared statement issued last night, Hon. Mr. Cullen said: "I find it difficult to believe that the Hon. Mr. Harkness made the statement attributed to him in a Canadian Press dispatch yesterday.
There are many potato growers in Prince Edward Island whose continued existence as farmers depend on the amount of assistance they receive in the disposal of the balance of their 1957 potato crop.
This unfortunate situation puts a grave responsibility on those whose duty it is to administer the Agricultural Stabilization Act, and we therefore expect from them statements which are carefully considered and supported by the record."
The record is as set out in this report:
"1. On June 3, I told the agricultural stabilization board that the province was prepared to provide for the administration of any plan that was acceptable to the growers.
2.	The first definite offer of a diversion program for P.E.I. was received on June 26 which was two days after Mr. Harkness announced in the press that we had been offered 36 cents a bushel for a feed diversion program.
3.	The application for a guaranteed price was made by a committee consisting of representatives of Prince Edward Island potato producers' association, the Prince Edward Island potato dealers' association, the potato promotion committee, the federation of agriculture and the P.E.I. marketing board."
No one would dare to say that those people do not know the condition or quality of the potatoes on the island. I continue:
"4. After receipt was confirmed by wire on June 26, any delay in accepting the miserable offer was due to the fact that the committee wished to make every effort possible to secure a better agreement before accepting an offer which at best would give the grower only a small part of his cost of production and which under present conditions proved to be worthless.

The only reason that the offer was accepted on July 7 was that the committee did not wish to deprive any grower of a chance to receive assistance, however small it might be.
In regard to Mr. Harkness' statement that island growers accepted the proposal, then discovered that the potatoes had sprouted, I wish to say that four days before the offer I sent Mr. Harkness a wire which stated that his offer was practically worthless because less than 15 per cent of island potatoes were firm at that date.
The offer was accepted only after I received an answer to my wire which stated that Mr. Harkness could see no reason for changing the conditions."
Fortunately, Mr. Chairman, a few hours after the minister had made this statement in the house an announcement was made in Charlottetown that the department, after representations were made from the potato growers association and from the government of Prince Edward Island, had modified their offer and I understand that now 75 per cent of the potatoes will be covered by this price support. My reason for putting on the record the information which I have placed there tonight was to answer the statement made by the minister, putting the entire blame on the government of Prince Edward Island and on the potato growers of the island.

That is why I feel that if the Department of Agriculture were willing to give an adequate publicity to that product, not only in the springtime, but the whole year round, we could hope that part at least of this product, if not all of it, would sell at reasonable prices in this country.
If it was required that all maple syrup marketed be clearly labelled "pure syrup", "artificial or falsified syrup", whatever the case may be, we could hope that the consumer, seeing the difference, would be inclined to secure pure syrup, even if its price were a little higher, and we are convinced that after one try, he would always insist on buying that delightful product of matchless flavour. Maple syrup production in this country has now passed the $10 million mark. I feel therefore that the government should bring an immediate solution to the marketing of this product, in close co-operation with the Quebec maple producers co-operative and the newly formed syndicate.
I also would like to suggest to the Minister of Agriculture to include in his credits some money for subsidizing the purchase of chemical fertilizer.
In various areas, the soil is not quite suitable for farming, and it is only with great effort and a great deal of pains that the settler, and later the farmer, succeed in making their land profitable, which often takes several years. That is why I feel that a subsidy of this kind would not only be an incentive, but a genuine help to all who have anything to do with farming.
I also believe that subsidies on the transportation of seed grain from the west to the east of this country should be increased, as an incitement to our farmers who would buy this grain. We would thus kill two birds with one stone, for while helping eastern farmers, we would promote the disposal of farm products from the west.
I could submit many more requests on behalf of our farmers, but I shall limit myself at this time to those I just mentioned. I must admit that I was somehow disappointed this afternoon when I heard the hon. member for Joliette-l'Assomption-Montcalm deal with farm problems in the light of political partisanship. To my mind, farming brings up issues important enough to be treated seriously by setting up the proper legislation that would help our farmers to solve them.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before proceeding to deal briefly with the suggestions I wish to bring before the committee tonight I wish to express the appreciation of this group for the courtesy, competence and good work of the departmental officials and the staff of the department throughout the country. These well-trained men and women perform a vital and essential service for Canada without any fanfare and, in most cases, without any publicity. I suppose we all recognize that major improvements in farm efficiency and production to a great extent depend on their intelligence, training and industry.
I think everyone will say that in the Department of Agriculture we have on the staff a good percentage who have all three of those requirements. Still, Mr. Chairman, our sense of values in this country is so unbalanced that in many cases a peanut vendor or a hot dog pedlar receives more compensation for a year's employment than do some of these highly trained, well-qualified and loyal public servants.
I am somewhat interested in this question, Mr. Chairman, because as a matter of fact I went to college in 1909 with a good number of former officials of the Department of Agriculture, and the forestry branch of another department, but unfortunately most of those officials have retired. I am one of the ancient remnants of that class still surviving in this house and who will survive for some time yet, I hope. Anyway, I urge the minister to do all he can to correct any salary injustices that are brought to his attention by the agricultural institute of Canada or by any other appropriate organization concerned with the welfare of these people and this staff.
Whenever I think of the good work done by these people who carry on their services largely unheard of, largely unsung and to some extent underpaid in some cases, I cannot help thinking of those lines in Gray's "Elegy in a Country Churchyard":
Full many a flower is bom to blush unseen,
And waste its sweetness on the desert air.
I think Mr. Minister, you will recollect the fact that you have two rather tall flowers in the department in Ottawa.
I am very much interested in these estimates because I come from generations of farmers and foresters in Great Britain primarily and in the last approximately 50 years in British Columbia. I have experienced all the vicissitudes that a green Englishman experiences in entering a virgin forest and converting it to orchards, grass-growing land, tillable soil and so on. I could tell you of some most

interesting experiences but I would rather do that when I am not taking the time of the house. However, I should like to say this in order to illustrate the tenacity, the purpose, the vigour and the intelligence of the early settlers who came out in my district in the upper Arrow lakes with very little money but great hopes, some of which have been shattered in the years succeeding. We were greatly interested in raising a fine breed of poultry and none of us had the money to invest in a really topnotch rooster. Do you know what we did? We all clubbed together and we had something that was very rare in Canada, on the upper Arrow lakes in the early days-we had a travelling rooster and we used to put him in a crate and transfer him from place to place, as the poultry farmers' requirements demanded.
In any event, I am speaking tonight on behalf of this group because this group is greatly concerned about the preservation of the family farm in the agricultural economy of Canada. This group views with concern the devitalization of our rural life in some areas, the decline of the family farm in other areas and the lack of opportunity provided for young people on the family farm, the lack of opportunity for the sons and daughters of Canadians who wish to farm and are capable of farming-and I have personal knowledge of a good number in my constituency-but who, owing to the conditions that prevail today, are unable to give vent to their desires and their hopes in that respect.
When we come to contemplate the millions ol dollars spent on defence and the millions of dollars spent in subsidizing industry-for instance, the gold mining industry; and that has been a necessary and temporary expedient in recent years-we cannot understand why we in this country cannot do something for the thousands of young Canadians who wish to farm at this time and are denied that opportunity. In the remarks I wish to make this evening I intend to suggest the necessity for national rational planning as the result of federal-provincial co-operation to undertake certain policies that we think are necessary to bring together our idle resources in land and our ambitious people who wish to take advantage of those resources.
The first requirement when you come to establish a farm is land. We have an abundance of that commodity in this country. Before passing on I want to say that I support very strongly-as does this group, as a matter of fact-the proposals of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture for a national conservation and rehabilitation act, to be applied for the purpose of moving people
Supply-Agriculture
from marginal farms on to good soil and developing the thousands and thousands of undeveloped and unused acres in this country.
Before proceeding further I want to say that I have followed with interest the committee in the other place which has been studying land use for some weeks, a continuation of the studies commenced last session. I think that committee is doing excellent work because they are hearing evidence from people who know something about this question. I advise any hon. member who is interested in this subject to read the minutes of the committee on land use that is being carried on in the other place.
To illustrate briefly-and this has some local application and no one can ever accuse me of talking for the folks back home; I am talking for Canada in general but I use local illustrations because I have personal knowledge of them-and to mention the opportunities in the thousands of acres that can be brought under cultivation, we have in the Kootenay district a valley known as the Lardeau valley. In that valley there are at the present time 16,000 acres of first class land that could be brought under production. At the present time a great amount of it is covered with timber. Quite a large extent of it requires draining. But under some national conservation or rehabilitation act there is an opportunity for the development of a large area of land, as a result of the co-operation between the federal government and provincial governments, for the placing of young Canadians who will live their lives as farmers.
Another valley is the Slocan valley which is over 31 miles long and with thousands of acres of land. Some of it requires draining, some of it requires irrigating and some of it requires clearing of a poor species of timber. This valley is very suitable for agriculture. It is about one and a half miles wide and 31 miles long and there is a paved highway down the centre. There is also a power line right through the centre of the valley and there is quite a large river of about a hundred feet in width flowing through the valley. It is good land with good roads, power and water, and everything required for successful agricultural development. All that is necessary is some co-operation on the part of the governments to bring it into production.
In this connection I would say that the Slocan valley agricultural and conservation association, of which I am very pleased to be a member, is very interested in this development and wrote to ask if I would take up with the minister the question of having

Supply-Agriculture
surveys made to determine the possibilities of the valley. This I did, and I want to express sincere appreciation on behalf of all those settlers of his interest in the matter and of his willingness to consider undertaking something of that sort if the provincial government would also show their interest in the matter and would make some representation in this connection to the federal government. I do hope the people back home will be able to get the provincial government to take the initial steps in this direction.
We also have the Inonoaklin valley which is 15 miles long and has thousands of acres of available land, in this case mostly under cultivation. All that is required there is transportation. They have the soil, they have the production, they have the farmers on the land and a good many farmers' sons who are anxious to farm. I know dozens of these young fellows who are not interested in going to university or gaining an academic education but who want to farm. However, because of the amount of capital required under present conditions they are unable to do so.
We also have some smaller areas throughout my constituency along the Kootenay lakes, the Arrow lakes, and Slocan lake which present opportunities for agricultural development. I have mentioned this matter as an indication of what we have in Canada. These areas I have outlined are in one constituency which is largely a mountainous constituency, so what opportunities must there be in other parts of this country? The first requirement is, of course, land and we have that in abundance -good land. The second requirement is young people who wish to farm, and we have those in good numbers. The third requirement, as I see it, is a satisfactory form of agricultural credit on a long term basis which will permit these young people to undertake a farming life without being oppressed by the necessity to repay loans in a relatively short period of time. There has been much experience in this connection in Great Britain and other European countries and anyone who has knowledge of long term agricultural credit knows that as far as land is concerned it can rarely stand an interest rate higher than 3 per cent to be repaid over a term of 30 years or more.
In that connection I would like to quote briefly from a document I received from the director of the Veterans' Land Act administration with respect to supervised farm credit. I want to give Brigadier Rutherford every credit for exercising some imagination and I think anyone with any knowledge

of what is being done under his administration, within the limited scope of the act and within the limited amount of credit permitted under the act, will agree that the administration has blazed a trail which we might follow with respect to the development of a sound agricultural policy in Canada.
I would like to read three paragraphs from this document, which are as follows:
Supervised Farm Credit for the Family-Sized Production-Line Farm by T. J. Rutherford
Supervised farm credit is not an entirely new idea. Something of this nature was tried out in western Canada by an association of lending institutions who were having serious difficulties with their farm accounts during the depression period. It has also been tried to a limited extent by some lending agencies in the United States. However, it remained for the veterans land administration to give it a name, and to put the idea to work on a wide base and in a manner which has demonstrated how very effective it can be made in "putting agricultural credit to its highest and best use, and in ensuring its repayment in the ordinary course of business and without tears."
Since the amount and value of the land, livestock and equipment required as components of an economic family farm unit continue to increase, the need for carefully supervised credit in just the right amount-no more no less-and made available at just the right time to competent and progressive farmers capable of using it to good advantage, becomes more and more urgent. In fact, it has now become a necessity if agriculture is to again take its place with other industries in the matter of income to those who work, manage and, at the same time, largely finance its production units-
Adequate Supervised Farm Credit a Necessity today
The provision of adequate supervised farm credit is undoubtedly the most effective way in which various levels of government can assist agriculture to correct the income differential as related to other industries and, at the same time, bring production more in line with future market requirements. While industrial corporations finance their production to a considerable extent with funds supplied by holders of bonds and preferred stocks- who, though not actively engaged in the business, have a first claim upon its assets and income as security for the credit advanced-farmers generally have no such source of credit. This disadvantage is one which government, at all levels, can help to remove by making adequate credit available to this basic industry under a type of supervision that will minimize risk of loss and ensure its highest and best use in the building up of economically sound family farm units-which are the backbone of a permanent, prosperous agriculture.
The capital requirements of those now engaged in agriculture are nearly three times greater, on a gainfully employed worker basis, than they are in other industries and at least three times greater than they were when the Veterans' Land Act was enacted in 1942. The lack of available capital is unquestionably responsible for much underemployment and uneconomic labour on Canadian farms-
And I can endorse that from experience.
-for the reason that many of these farms are too small and/or inadequately equipped and stocked to constitute sound, economic units. Larger and better units would, of course, mean fewer units, and also the taking out of agriculture and putting

back into trees of considerable submarginal land and, in some cases, packets of reasonably good land that are too small, badly situated or scattered to be assembled into economic farm units under present conditions.
I think Brigadier Rutherford has stated the case very well indeed and I would just like to quote briefly from the table he mentions which shows the value of supervised farm credit. This table is as follows:
Net worth-The average net worth of the settlers, including the conditional grant of $2,320 as if earned at time of settlement	$5,117
The average net worth, December, 1957, an average of 8.3 years after settlement	$13,433
In view of the limited capital available and the situation under which many of these men commenced farming, I think this is very creditable indeed and is a clear indication of what could be done by an expansion of this form of supervised farm credit at low interest rates over a period of up to 40 years which is very badly needed.
The other day when the Canadian Farm Loan Act amendment was under consideration I did not take advantage of the opportunity to discuss this question because I thought I would be ruled out of order and my remarks on that act, therefore, were very few indeed. It was however obvious from the debate-and this applies to the remarks of many members from all parties in this house-that there was a great deal of dissatisfaction with respect to the adequacy of the present Canadian Farm Loan Act. I am not criticizing the commissioners or the officials-they are there to administer the act and the regulations-but the whole basis of the act makes it necessary that they administer it as a mortgage company would administer a loan, on a strictly, shall I say, mortgage company basis, expecting practically the rate of interest required by a mortgage company without any direct supervision of the operation of the farm and the attitudes towards loans are the attitudes of the mortgage companies, investment houses and institutions of that sort.
I am sure that during the debate the minister will be convinced of the necessity for exercising some imagination to bring together the land and the young people who wish to farm, many of whom are the sons and in some cases the daughters of men who fought for this country in the first world war, or the second world war, or both, because we have some pretty vigorous war veterans from the first world war, as evidence given before the veterans committee has shown.
Further, I think we need a national form of crop insurance. I was pleased to hear the minister say recently that the matter was being given close study. I do not for
Supply-Agriculture
a moment underestimate the difficulties, particularly when one has to deal with all the ten provinces and take into account the different attitudes towards this type of legislation. But the need is obvious, the matter is urgent, and it is one which requires the co-operation of federal and provincial departments of agriculture and governments if this problem is to be met.
I am not suggesting for a moment that crop insurance will cure all the ills of agriculture. Some of the present ills can be cured by irrigation, some by satisfactory under-drainage, some by better tillage, but regardless of a farmer's efficiency in these directions there are still the hazards of weather, disease and insects. I see no reason why we should not, as Churchill said on one occasion, make the law of averages come to the rescue of millions in this country with respect to crop insurance which is so necessary.
I am quite sure that if the Minister of Agriculture wants to have some evidence of the success of crop insurance in a limited sphere he could do no better than study the hail insurance plan introduced by the British Columbia fruit growers association. I might say that this is not the only progressive step which has been undertaken by this association. We were the first fruit growers organization to fight for marketing legislation on a provincial basis, and the first agricultural organization of this type, I think, to establish a form of crop insurance with hail insurance. While that act is limited in scope I think it shows what can be done and if we can get the federal government and provincial governments with the farmer's associations and the farmers, whether wheat growers, or fruit growers or hog raisers working together, surely we have the intelligence to devise an act which will protect the farmers of Canada against the vicissitudes of nature.
Another field which I think is certainly
worthy of investigation by the minister and by the government is the need for more satisfactory transportation. As I mentioned before, I have one valley in my area, the Inonoaklin valley which has a very good production record, but which lacks direct access to the markets by road. I do think that the federal government together with the provincial government of British Columbia should give thought to the development of such highways as are required to bring agricultural commodities to the centres of population. We hear a lot about the tourist trade and the necessity for building highways to assist these visitors, but I do think that the needs of farmers in certain areas

Supply-Agriculture
deserve more attention by federal and provincial governments on a co-operative basis so that they may be provided with transportation facilities which up to now have been denied.
One other matter which I should like to discuss is the question of unemployment insurance for farm workers. As the minister knows, the British Columbia fruit growers association has repeately passed resolutions in recent years urging that the Unemployment Insurance Act be amended so as to provide unemployment insurance for farm workers. I know that the failure of the government to do that has resulted in hardship to farmers in Canada. I have personal knowledge of a number of farmers who are unable to obtain labour for short periods, for which they are willing to pay industrial wages, because the men who might have accepted employment would not be building up unemployment insurance contributions. As a result, labour was simply not available for gathering fruit, making hay, and harvesting other crops, because, as I say, workers on farms are not covered by unemployment insurance. I would urge the minister to discuss this matter with his colleague the Minister of Labour.

I am glad to hear that these discussions have been undertaken, and I hope that at least in the course of next session-I am not one of those who are advocating that too much legislation should come forward during this session from now on-the minister will introduce amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act to deal with the points I have raised. I am happy to know that we have had such a good influence on the minister.
In addition,-and I know this is primarily a matter for the provincial governments-I hope consideration will be given to making workmen's compensation available to farmers under better circumstances than now exist in most provinces at the present time.
An investment in rural life will, I am certain, pay dividends in national stability, in happiness for many people, and in cash for those concerned as well as for the governments who have control over the affairs of this country. I am a great supporter of rural life because I believe that for a nation to be strong, progressive and healthy and to continue to be democratic in every sense of the word we must have a strong, well organized
TMr. Herridge.]
rural population who are making their living on the land, not only because they love to do it but because the return provided is a fair share of the national income.
We have an excellent staff in the Department of Agriculture. I know that so far as British Columbia is concerned they have excellent people there. I have met a good many of these chaps at different times and they would be only too willing to feel that they were taking part in a well-designed, well-planned national policy with a particular purpose in mind, as a result of co-operation between the federal government, provincial governments, farmers' organizations and the farmers themselves.
Every one in the chain of responsibility should accept some responsibility in support of a national plan. As far as this group is concerned it is the only road we should travel in the future if we are going to achieve the success that is necessary. These things are required to ensure the continued operation, preservation and development of this very vital sector of our economy, the Canadian family farm.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ALLOWANCE AND EXTEND BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I feel I would not be performing my duty at this time if I did not make a few remarks concerning agriculture. The subject of agriculture has always been very close to my heart. I am the third generation in my family to follow agriculture and I have three sons engaged in it at the present time.
I have been connected with farm organizations for about 15 years and as a result of this experience I have learned something of the problems that affect agriculture in every province in Canada including Ontario. We have heard a considerable amount of discussion about agriculture and particularly about western agriculture but not too much has been said about the industry in the east.
I listened with much interest and a certain amount of pleasure to the Minister of Agriculture when he made his remarks on Friday, July 11, 1958. At that time I was prompted to ask myself if agriculture is in the rosy haze of prosperity about which we have heard so much or, on the other hand, if there are some very important aspects of agriculture in a critical position to which we are attempting to blind ourselves and make ourselves believe they do not exist. I should like to explain what I mean by these statements and perhaps I can best do so by asking this question. Are we, as members of parliament, satisfied with the over-all picture of agriculture today? We must remember that agriculture is the oldest industry in

the world. It is the life blood of this generation and of generations still unborn. It is the foundation upon which we have built up this land of ours.
I quite agree with the statement made by the minister when he said the total income of agriculture is much higher than it was a year ago. It is gratifying and a source of some satisfaction to know that this has occurred under the able leadership of the present minister but obviously it could have a detrimental effect on all agriculture if we do not explain to the consuming public the exact position in which agriculture finds itself. Most people scorn the thought of any assistance being given to agriculture. When we talk about increased protection from imports the consumer feels that agriculture is already in a prosperous condition and not in need of further consideration. I believe it is the responsibility of those who are dependent on agriculture for their livelihood to present a true picture of the industry and the position in which we find it.
When discussing the position of the farmer and his wife and family with an intelligent consumer a few days ago I was informed by him that there was plenty of money on the farm and that farming was a secure position. The consumer suggested that if the farmer did not like his position in agriculture he should get out of it and take up something else. I believe that is the feeling of a great many people who are not engaged in the agricultural industry. Those engaged in the industry must remember that they represent only a small percentage of the total population, about 12 per cent at the present time. There are, therefore, eight people looking for cheap food as compared with one who is trying to secure a fair return for his labour in this field of endeavour.
We have heard a great deal about the wheat situation and I can assure you that wheat is an important part of Canada's agricultural industry but there are other sections of the industry which are equally important. As long as we have a surplus of western grains we are going to have trouble in agriculture. We want to make it prosperous for the wheat farmer to be able to sell his wheat and continue selling wheat. Just as soon as it becomes unprofitable for him to do that he will engage in some other line of production such as livestock in which we have a surplus at the present time.
I fully agree with the following statement of the Saskatchewan wheat pool taken from one of its publications:
Other exporters, such as the United States and France, directly subsidize their exports of wheat and flour. More recently the United States has
Supply-Agriculture
offered a variety of inducements such as long term credits, barter deals and give-aways to Induce importers to buy their wheat.
The combination of import restrictions and export subsidies which are now almost universal in the wheat trade force the Canadian farmer into competition with foreign governments. So far, the Canadian farmer has met this competition virtually unaided. In requesting deficiency payments he is asking the government of Canada to help bear part of this burden of unfair competition.
At the present time the wheat farmer should be given some sort of support in selling his wheat at a profit to enable him to remain in the business of growing and selling wheat regardless of how this is done. I feel that every one from eastern Canada should be concerned about the situation and offer the western farmer every support.
The September 1957 issue of The Rural Scene published by John Atkins Publishing Company Limited in Midland, Ontario, contains an interesting article, a portion of which I wish to place on the record:
We believe that Mr. Diefenbaker is actuated by a sincere desire to give Canada good government, and by an equally sincere desire to preserve Canadian agriculture as a self-dependent, self-respecting industry.
We believe that, if he discovers that some of his pre-election promises were hastily made and without a clear realization of all they implied, and if a closer study of the problems convinces him that some of his promised remedies are likely to do more harm than good, he will not hesitate to do what is in the best interests of the country and of the farming industry, rather than what is closest to the letter of his promises.
In this he should have the full support of all parties in the house.
I am sure there are not many hon. members who feel that agriculture has been promised too much. Another article in the same issue bears the title "The Market Price is Starting Point" and reads in part as follows:
Minister of Agriculture Harkness is said to be studying the question of a fair price-cost relationship for farm products.
In such a study the first thing to determine is what would be a fair price for any product.
The answer to this question can be found in the decision of Mr. Justice W. J. Schwenger last December in a dairy arbitration case. The item reads:-
"The gross value of 100 pounds of milk is not its cost of production under normal conditions, but what it will bring on the available market. The net worth of 100 pounds of milk must be this gross return less all expenses of shipping and processing."
If that applies to agriculture, why should it not apply to every industry? How many industries today throw their products on the market at whatever prices they will bring? Agriculture should be in a position no different from that of any other industry. The farmer must have his cost of production plus a reasonable rate of return on his investment. It is this kind of thing that is poisoning the

Supply-Agriculture
consuming public against the thought of giving any consideration to agriculture. I continue reading from the same article:
No article of commerce has any value other than what it will bring on the market. The government's duty is to see that nothing interferes with the free functioning of the market, for the judgment of the market is the judgment of all interested parties.
In the same issue of this publication under the heading "Time to Define Farm Prosperity" we find this significant statement:
The question arises: If the Canadian taxpayers have to furnish 75 per cent of the capital the farmers need, and also have to give the farmer-controlled marketing hoards monopolies in the Canadian market, and, on top of that, if they have to pay higher taxes to support farm prices at levels satisfactory to the farmers, of what benefit would the agricultural industry be to the country? It would be a mendicant industry, living on what it could get out of the government and not on the value of its service to the people.
By no stretch of the imagination could it be called a truly prosperous, self-supporting, self-respecting industry.
I am sure no one in the agricultural industry is looking for a handout or for any support that is not due to him. These statements should be corrected so that the consuming public will know the conditions we are facing at the present time. I have another quotation that I should like to put on the record:
We have all heard of the recently discovered Parkinson's law, which says that, in the government service, work will always be stretched out to occupy all the time available for its completion.
The same law seems to apply to costs when the government is paying them.
The article goes on to say that agriculture is a high-cost producing industry, unable to compete in the free market without help from the government. I continue:
More and more our farmers are looking to the governments to solve their problems for them. More and more they are depending on their political influence and less on their farming abilities.
I do not think there are many farmers who try to drag out the cost of production so that they will have more grounds on which to apply for assistance from the government.
I would like to say a word about the stabilization bill that was brought in last year. It is one of the things that we should be proud of. I think it is the answer to our agricultural problem but there have to be amendments made to it from time to time. We have adopted some support prices. In some instances some of us think they are not high enough; others think they are too high. However, it is a step in the right direction, and if it is carefully handled it can prove to be of great assistance to agriculture.
We have heard a great deal about inefficiency. To me it has got to be a poor excuse for not giving consideration to agriculture.

Most of our farmers are efficient. I feel that there are many other industries that have not proved as efficient as agriculture. It is true that we have the odd farmer who is not so efficient, but by and large our farmers are certainly producing as much as and probably more than anyone in any other industry.
I did say something about wheat, but we must consider that world wheat trade is down. It has been dropping year by year not because of the fact that we have not been getting markets but because other things are affecting us along this line. According to the IFAP News one of the reasons for:
-reduced wheat imports needs in many countries, especially western Europe; reduced export supplies in several countries including-
Many of the larger producing countries have give-away and barter programs that are being conducted throughout the world. We have assisted through the Colombo plan a number of those countries which were importing our wheat a few years ago. Through better agricultural programs, tile draining, draining of land, insecticides and many other things, they have increased the yield of food in those countries many, many times. It is good that we have done that, but in doing that we have reduced some of our wheat exports. Again, the consumption of wheat, or of the products of wheat, has undergone a change. The eating habits of people throughout Canada today have changed. They are not eating as many products made from wheat flour. Therefore, a change should be made in the program but we must be careful that we do not bring it on too quickly and upset our whole agricultural program.
I would like to say a word about the beef industry with which I have been connected very closely for a number of years. It is quite true that we are getting a fair price for our beef cattle today but there should be a word of caution to those people who are thinking of getting into the beef industry. As long as we can export our surplus beef to the United States, as long as there is a demand for it, we are going to have a fair beef price; but just as soon as they get enough of our cattle the price will fall back to where it was before. Most of us realize that the United States would not be importing quite as much as they are importing at the present time if it were not for the drought conditions they have experienced in certain areas. Because of that their cattle population has been dwindling and therefore they want our cattle. But I would caution a number of people who are thinking of getting out of the dairy industry and into the beef industry. They might find that it will not be so profitable in a few years time.

I wish to say something about our hog production and our hog industry. We have been favoured with a good price for pork in the last year. I hope it will continue, but I am very doubtful whether we are not going to get into over-production. One of the greatest difficulties that we have in the agricultural and livestock industry at the present time, and that includes the hog industry, is the vertical integration and the contract feeding. We have quite a trend toward it in the province of Ontario and if something is not done to correct it we are going to put most of the small farmers out of existence. According to the pamphlet on hogs which I hold in my hand, in the United States 60,000 farmers with 100 sows, each farrowing twice a year, could produce 96 million hogs and the total consumption there is around 89 million hogs. In Canada we are consuming about 6 million hogs in a year. About 375,000 sows, averaging eight pigs twice a year, could produce all the pork that we need in Canada or about 3750 farmers would supply all the needs we have for pork products.
We had a vote in Ontario last Friday. There are 78,000 registered voters in Ontario alone. When we talk about setting up support prices I wonder who we are going to support. We talk about the cost of production. Nobody knows the cost of production. Most of us who have been engaged in agriculture for a number of years do not need too many economists to tell us what it costs to produce a hog, or the cost of production of most of the products on our farms; but if we are to set up a support price that will be an incentive to the large producers or to the feed dealers or the man who is setting up a hog farm, who can buy his grain at wholesale prices, who can buy his concentrates at wholesale prices, he will not care whether he makes too much on a hog. If he makes a dollar apiece and produces 5,000 hogs he will have $5,000; whereas the average small producer who produces a hundred hogs at a dollar apiece will receive only $100. I have heard something along that line. I know one producer in my own area who is building today and setting up a contract for 10,000 hogs a year with one of the large packers who will supply the feed. This is something that we must take a look at and not wait until the industry is in trouble before we correct this situation.
I would like to say a word about the dairy industry which is very important in Ontario, Quebec and the maritimes. We are very proud that we have a stabilization board. We have a support price under butter and cheese. Sometimes we have found that the support price becomes the ceiling. I have had numerous complaints and requests from
Supply-Agriculture
the cheese producers this year when they were in trouble. The Ontario cheese producers association was able to get a licence to buy cheese and in the past few weeks they have been stepping on the market and buying cheese. At the present time they have been able to raise the price to 35 cents, which is only a cent above last year. If they had not been able to do that the result would have been that the cheese price would have been one cent below last year.
The minister has suggested that they reduce the price of powdered milk from 17 cents to 15 cents. Seventeen cents was the price arrived at last year as the cost of a pound of powder and it seems to me that with the cost of production going up the price should have remained at that figure. I do not think many industries would have accepted a reduction, and with the experience I have had in agriculture I quite agree with the statement made by Lord Boyd Orr, a former FAO director general, when he said that it is difficult to prevent surpluses by reducing prices because the farmer with capital increases his output to compensate for the reduced price in an attempt to maintain his income. I quite agree with that statement because when I was farming in the thirties I know that to meet my expenses and taxes I had to produce a little bit more when we were producing at a very low figure. In those years I produced hogs for $3.25. I think we have got to adopt some policy that will give a fair return to agriculture. We can control our surplus position by other means than reducing prices.
In the dairy industry you have a complicated set-up because you have the whole milk producer enjoying prices that range from $4.90 to $5.60 a hundred and on the next farm you have a farmer producing milk for cheese for $2.40 or a farmer producing milk for butter at about the same figure. I hope we can find some way of putting a guaranteed price under all manufactured milk. Maybe that will bring us closer to the pooling of all milk so that everyone in the dairy industry can get a fair return. There are a lot of people in the whole milk business who would not like that. However, I am a whole milk producer myself and I am quite convinced that if we had that type of program the farmers in the whole milk industry today would be getting more money because they would not have the extra surpluses they are dumping into some other product causing other surpluses and their over-all picture would be much better than it is at the present time.
I want to say something about the fruit and vegetable growers because a number of people in my riding are involved. We had

Supply-Agriculture
a problem there a few weeks ago in connection with the dumping of raspberries on our market. There are a number of canning factories in my area which were canning raspberries. They had negotiated a price of 28 cents with the producers. I have a telegram I received from these people about a week ago which reads as follows:
-processor gave marketing board till 12 noon today at Brighton to decide to take 22 cents a quart which is below cost of production or they would import balance of pack. This means a reduction of 13 cents from last year.
They were going to import from New York state. The marketing board, rather than lose the opportunity of disposing of the berries, reduced the price to 22 cents. That is not going to result in jam or berries being a cent cheaper to the consumer. The price was negotiated at 28 cents and it is on that basis that the retail price will probably be decided. On the other hand, we cannot blame the processor too much because we allow canned goods to come in from the United States and he has to compete with them. Therefore, in order to compete he must secure his pack as cheaply as he can.
In my riding we have seven canning factories in Prince Edward county that are closed. Many people will say they are closed because they were inefficient. That is not the case. These factories were efficient. When they were Canadian Canners' factories they were efficient but when they were bought by California Packers they were immediately closed and the farmers lost their contracts. Each one of these factories had a payroll of some $200,000. That is gone and these people have nothing else to turn to. I understand that today Canadian Canners are operating two factories east of Toronto and two factories west of Toronto. They are importing whatever they need from California Packers and most of our stores today have the Del Monte brand of canned goods on their shelves. These are some of the things we must try to guard against.
Under the former government we lost many privileges because of the fact that concessions were given to other industries at the expense of agriculture and it is the former government that is responsible for the conditions we have today. It is very difficult for the present government to correct the situation in a short time. At the same time the opposition criticizes higher protection. I think it is up to all of us, whether on the government or opposition side of the house, to take a look at this picture.
It is not a small group that we are trying to protect but part of our agricultural industry. It has increased in size considerably

in the last two years. The increased consumption of canned fruits and vegetables in Canada has not resulted in benefits to the producer in this country. The benefit of increased consumption has gone to United States canners who have been able to dump their product in this country.
I discussed this matter some time ago with Mr. West, the assistant United States agricultural attache. We discussed ways and means of correcting the situation and I quite agree that we should sit down with these people and discuss the situation. It is not a case of increasing our tariffs to the extent that we will restrict trade but I think we should sit down with the United States processors and producers and negotiate ways and means of correcting this situation. I understand that the processors over there will have a surplus and some jobber will come along, buy a job lot and then, because the door is wide open, dump it into Canada and make a large profit. That kind of thing is hurting us considerably.
I can remember very well sitting down last year with a delegation in the United States and discussing some of the problems affecting our trade. I think the discussion went a long way in helping to understand the situation. Mr. West mentioned this when I was talking to him not very long ago. That is one suggestion I should like to offer that might help to improve the situation.
A lot of people are criticizing subsidizing everything, but when we take a look at what is happening in every country in the world with which we have to compete we see that the picture is quite different. I have here the newsletter published by the dairy farmers of Canada in which there is reference to the United Kingdom price of butter. Butter in Great Britain is the cheapest it has been in some 30 years and the price of butter in Britain is seriously affecting the New Zealand producer. Why is it affecting the New Zealand producer? The New Zealand producer is affected because Finland is putting her butter into Britain at a much lower price than before. The price of butter in Britain was 32 cents a year ago and now it is down to 23 cents. I should like to read hon. members an extract about the high dairy and poultry export subsidies in Finland.
USDA Foreign Crops and Markets reports that export subsidies paid by the Finnish government for dairy and poultry products-

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a few remarks to offer with regard to agricultural research. If I am not mistaken, the Department of Agriculture has a division with two research services included. The science service is concerned with purely scientific research, where specialists carry out, for instance, research in entomology, to prevent destruction of crops by insects, or on weeds, so as to improve the quality of crops, etc. The experimental farm services is concerned with research in more directly agricultural matters, experts in these fields carrying out research, at experimental farms, on improved methods of production of certain commodities, for instance on the most economical way of producing eggs or milk, soil specialization, etc.
If I understand correctly the annual cost of these two services is $10,000,000 in each case, which is $20,000,000 in all.
I wish to bring to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) a very important point. I feel that if we are to improve the efficiency of agriculture in this country, in the west as well as in the eastern and central parts of this country, we should at once adjust our research procedure. Let us set up a new co-ordination of existing services and give a new, bold and forward looking impulse to these research services, so as to develop ways to increase the income of the farmer who is now caught in the cost-price squeeze.
I will now proceed to put a few suggestions forward for the benefit of the Minister of Agriculture. These suggestions appear to have a great deal of interest for agriculture in general. However, before doing so, I would like to pay tribute to the former minister of agriculture in the preceding government who has, during his term of office, put into the hands of the farmers of this country production facilities which are without parallel anywhere else in the world.
When we were in power, we had, first of all, to look after the production problems, but we have also established a research system. And I note today that, since the Conservatives have been in power, no improvement has been made to that research system which was an initiative of the Liberal government.
Today, the selling at a loss of our farm products on the world markets is perhaps the most serious problem in Canada. The time
Supply-Agriculture
has come, I believe, to consider the situation realistically. We should not hesitate a moment to spend millions of dollars more to find, by means of all known scientific methods, the various uses to which our farm products could be put, in addition to ordinary consumption, local and foreign.
Only scientific research applied to our agricultural products under new forms, could, in my opinion, considerably contribute to increase our agricultural production. The day is coming, and very rapidly-and I believe we should hasten the coming of that day- where industry will become the greatest consumer of our agricultural products.
Thanks to scientific research, Mr. Chairman, there is no limit to our hopes. However, when we consider our achievements in this field, compared to what is being done in some foreign countries where production is similar to ours, we have to admit that we are lagging behind. It is interesting to consider what the United States are achieving in this field.
I should like here to quote an extract from the Manitoba Co-Operator of November 21, 1957. It is from an editorial entitled:
(Text):

Some months ago the United States Department of Agriculture announced its decision to increase its agricultural research budget to $50 million, an announcement welcomed by agriculture and industry alike, but one greeted in some quarters by criticism that the amount was too small and nearly twenty years too late.
The article proceeds further, talks about larger crops and surpluses and then continues as follows:
These mounting surpluses in both Canada and the United States point to the very great need for increased research, to find new uses for farm products. As one United States research worker points out "Science has given agriculture an almost limitless productive capacity, and therewith one of its biggest problems-control or utilization of surplus production. At the same time, it is on its way to solving that problem by finding not only new uses for agriculture products, but new farm crops that will be used only in industry".
Progress reported.

ARMED FORCES, FOREIGN SERVICE  FAMILY INCOME REDUCTIONS
speechtext:
1.	With respect to families of the following ranks: brigadier, lieutenant colonel, sergeant, private (a) with wife and three children; (b) with wife and five children, what is the net reduction in family income, during a four year tour of service outside Canada due to loss of family allowance after adjustment for any tax saving?
2.	What is the average reduction in family income in each case?
Answer by: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of
National Defence):
1.	Under the Family Allowances Act, administered by the Department of National Health and Welfare, family allowances are not payable to children residing outside of Canada. The loss of income would depend on the age of the children and the total income, including any income from sources other than employment in the forces. It is not possible, therefore, to provide a specific answer with respect to loss of income for each of the cases listed.
2.	Foreign allowances and living allowances paid to servicemen overseas would in the majority of cases exceed any reduction in family income due to discontinuance of family allowances while the children reside outside of Canada.

Question No. 165-Mr. Bell (Saint John-
Albert):
1.	Has an official investigation been conducted into the recently discovered wreckage of a small Royal Canadian Air Force aircraft near Juniper, New Brunswick, believed crashed on September 14, 1939, an a flight from Megantic, Quebec, to Sydney, Nova Scotia?
2.	If so, what is the official report of this investigation?
Answer by: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of
National Defence):
1.	Yes.
2.	Following a report of the sighting of a wrecked aircraft on July 9, 1958, an investigation was conducted by personnel of the R.C.M.P. and the R.C.M.P. It was established that the wreckage was Northrop Delta aircraft 673 which apparenty crashed on September 14, 1939, 40 miles from Fredericton, N.B.
Investigating officers have conducted a thorough ground search of the surrounding area and they have located a number of items which indicate that the crew, WOI Doan and Cpl. Rennie perished with the aircraft.
It is not considered that any useful purpose would be served by a further technical investigation into the cause of this accident because of the long interval, the condition of the wreckage and the lack of information on the flight.
